extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced graduate students in geometric analysis / Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Statements and structural/estimate results about three-dimensional ancient κ-solutions and related curvature/volume/neck/canonical-neighborhood properties in the Ricci flow (Perelman/Hamilton framework). Covers classification, noncollapsing, elliptic-type estimates, compactness, global structure, and the canonical neighborhood theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 6.3.3 (Perelman) — curvature upper bound from volume lower bound (part i)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every w>0 there exist B(w)<+∞, C=C(w)<+∞ such that: Suppose gij(t) is a (not necessarily complete) solution to the Ricci flow defined on M × [−t0 r0^2, 0] with the metric ball Bt(x0,r0) compactly contained in M for each t in the interval. If at each time t ∈ [−t0 r0^2, 0] we have Rm(.,t) ≥ −(r0)^{−2} on Bt(x0,r0) and Vol_t(Bt(x0,r0)) ≥ w r0^n, then for 0 < t ≤ t0 r0^2 and whenever dt(x,x0) ≤ r0/4, there holds |Rm(x,t)| ≤ C r0^{−2} + B (t + t0 r0^2)^{−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constants B and C depend only on w and dimension; statement obtained by scaling r0=1 in proof. The theorem is used to derive curvature upper bounds from local lower volume bounds; proof uses contradiction, blow-up, and Perelman's compactness/ancient-solutions contradiction arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 6.3.3 (Perelman) — curvature & volume control from initial volume bound (part ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same setup, if additionally for some 0 < tau (bar tau) ≤ t0 we have Rm(x,t) ≥ −(r0)^{−2} for t ∈ [−bar_tau r0^2, 0], x ∈ Bt(x0,r0), and Vol_0(B0(x0,r0)) ≥ w r0^n, then there exist ξ = ξ(w)>0 and τ0 = τ0(w)>0 and constants B(w),C(w) so that for all t with max{bar_tau r0^2, τ0 r0^2} ≤ t ≤ 0 and for dt(x,x0) ≤ r0/4 one has |Rm(x,t)| ≤ C r0^{−2} + B (t + t0 r0^2)^{−1} and Vol_t(Bt(x0,r0)) ≥ ξ r0^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (ii) strengthens (i) when a prior volume bound at time 0 is given; gives a uniform positive volume lower bound at later times as well as curvature estimates. Constants depend only on w and dimension. Proof uses continuity, relative volume comparison, and the estimate from part (i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 6.4.1 — classification of 3D gradient shrinking Ricci solitons
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (M,gij(t)) be a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton on a three-manifold with bounded and nonnegative sectional curvature and κ-noncollapsed on all scales for some κ>0. Then (M,gij(t)) is one of: (i) the round three-sphere S^3 or a metric quotient of S^3; (ii) the round infinite cylinder S^2 × R, or one of its Z_2 quotients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits cases: nonstrictly positive sectional curvature leads (after passing to universal cover and maximum principle) to S^2×R quotients; strictly positive compact case tends to round space form so is S^3 or quotient; noncompact strictly positive case is excluded by analysis using f (potential), level sets, curvature growth and Gauss-Bonnet contradiction. This classification is used to characterize possible blow-up limits and to deduce universal noncollapsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6.4.2 — universal noncollapsing
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a positive constant κ0 such that any nonflat three-dimensional ancient κ-solution (for some κ>0) is either κ0-noncollapsed on all scales or is a metric quotient of the round three-sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: take basepoint p and Perelman's l-function and reduced volume V(τ); extract asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton limits of scalings at times τ → ∞; show limiting soliton has bounded curvature (otherwise produce splitting contradicting curvature properties); by Lemma 6.4.1 limiting soliton must be S^3-quotient or cylinder; if not S^3-quotient then conclude a uniform positive lower bound on volumes (Perelman's reduced volume arguments) yielding κ0. The proposition gives a universal noncollapsing constant for all nonflat ancient κ-solutions unless they are round-sphere quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 6.4.3 (Elliptic type estimate) — scale and derivative control (part i)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist positive η and an increasing function ω such that: for any three-dimensional ancient κ-solution (M,gij(t)) (0< t < +∞? — the statement uses t in (−∞,0]) and any x,y ∈ M and time t in the solution interval, R(x,t) ≤ R(y,t) · ω(R(y,t) d_t(x,y)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a quantitative relation controlling curvature at one point by curvature at another in terms of scaled squared distance; ω depends only on κ and dimension indirectly (through constants). The proof uses universal noncollapsing (Proposition 6.4.2), Li-Yau-Hamilton Harnack, local curvature/volume estimates (Theorem 6.3.3), and derivative estimates (Shi) to obtain a control function ω.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 6.4.3 (Elliptic type estimate) — derivative bounds (part ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist η>0 such that for all x and t in a three-dimensional ancient κ-solution one has |∇R|(x,t) ≤ η R^{3/2}(x,t) and |∂R/∂t|(x,t) ≤ η R^2(x,t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are local derivative (elliptic-type) estimates derived from (i), the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and Shi's local derivative estimates. η is a universal constant depending only on κ and dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 6.4.4 — compactness of ancient κ0-solutions modulo scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of nonflat three-dimensional ancient κ0-solutions is compact modulo scaling: for any sequence of such solutions and marked points (x_k,0) with R(x_k,0)=1 one can extract a subsequence converging in C^∞_loc to an ancient κ0-solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Theorem 6.4.3(i) to get uniform control, Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, and Hamilton's compactness theorem. One must rule out unbounded curvature in the limit by blow-up arguments and splitting theorems which would contradict Proposition 6.1.1; hence the limit has bounded curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / criterion — center of an evolving ε-neck
rubrics_metrics.description: A point x0 at time t=0 is called the center of an evolving ε-neck if, letting Q = R(x0,0), the solution on the parabolic region { (x',t'): t' ∈ [−ε^{−1} Q^{−1}, 0], d_t(x',x0) < ε^{−1} Q^{−1/2} } after scaling by factor Q and shifting time so t maps to 0, is ε-close in C^{[ε^{−1}]} topology to the corresponding subset of the evolving round cylinder with scalar curvature 1 at time 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the geometric/analytic notion of an ε-neck used to classify local geometry; closeness is in high C^k norms after parabolic rescaling. This notion underpins the canonical neighborhood statements and the identification of 'neck' regions in noncompact ancient solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 6.4.5 (Perelman) — global structure of noncompact ancient κ-solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: For any ε>0 there exists C(ε)>0 such that: if g_ij(t) is a nonflat ancient κ-solution on a noncompact three-manifold M and M_ε denotes points not centers of evolving ε-necks at t=0, then either M is the round cylinder S^2×R or its Z_2 quotients, or: (i) M_ε is compact; (ii) diam(M_ε) ≤ C Q^{−1/2} and C^{−1} Q ≤ R(x,0) ≤ C Q for all x ∈ M_ε, where Q = R(x0,0) for some x0 ∈ ∂M_ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof distinguishes the case of nontrivial null curvature vector (giving cylinder or quotient) and the positive-curvature case (where M is diffeomorphic to R^3). Uses Theorem 6.4.3 to show faraway points are neck centers, compactness arguments to enclose M_ε by a finite region, a blow-up contradiction to bound diam(M_ε) relative to Q and to bound scalar curvature on M_ε. C depends only on ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 6.4.6 (Canonical neighborhood theorem) — local classification of neighborhoods
rubrics_metrics.description: For any ε>0 there exist positive constants C1(ε), C2(ε) with the following property: Suppose (M,gij(x,t)) is a three-dimensional nonflat ancient κ-solution. Then either the solution is the round RP^3×R (RP^3 with R?), or every point (x,t) has an open neighborhood B = B_t(x,r) with r < C1 R(x,t)^{−1/2} and B_t(x,2r) ⊂ B_t(x, r) which falls into one of three categories: (a) an evolving ε-neck (parabolic region is ε-close to evolving round cylinder after scaling); (b) an evolving ε-cap (time slice at t of an evolving metric on B^3 or RP^3 minus a compact set modeled on an ε-neck); (c) [the chunk ends before (c) is fully stated].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Perelman's canonical neighborhood description: every point at appropriate scale is either neck-like, cap-like, or in a high-curvature compact region modeled on positively curved space-forms (complete classification continues beyond the chunk). Constants C1,C2 depend only on ε; this theorem is used to analyze singularity models and surgery regions.
